A prognostic model was developed and validated using electronic health records (EHRs) from 10 NHS trusts in the UK, including 25 665 patients diagnosed between 1998 and 2014.
FINDINGS: The model achieved a mean leave-one-trust-out C statistic of 0.71 (95% CI 0.68–0.75) for predicting clozapine initiation, with a positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.15 (95% CI 0.12–0.17) and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96 (95% CI 0.95–0.97). When using a broader TR definition (clozapine or ≥3 antipsychotics), discrimination dropped to a C statistic of 0.68 (95% CI 0.64–0.72), with PPV 0.27 (95% CI 0.24–0.31) and NPV 0.89 (95% CI 0.88–0.91).
INTERPRETATION: The model shows acceptable discrimination for predicting clozapine initiation, particularly in ruling out future TR (high NPV), but modest PPV suggests many predicted cases may not develop TR. Strengths include large, real-world EHR data and external validation across multiple trusts. Limitations include reliance on clozapine initiation as a proxy for TR, potential unmeasured confounding, and lack of clinical outcome validation beyond medication exposure. The effect size is statistically meaningful but not large enough to guide individual treatment decisions without further refinement.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This model could support early identification of patients at higher risk of TR, potentially enabling earlier clozapine initiation. However, current performance metrics suggest it should be used as an adjunct to clinical judgment rather than a standalone decision tool. Further validation in prospective settings and evaluation of clinical impact are needed.

item.title: [7] Adaptation and Pilot Testing of a Mindfulness-Based Insomnia and Symptom Management Intervention for Women with Breast Cancer in Rural Areas.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This study adapted and pilot-tested a mindfulness-based insomnia and symptom management intervention (Nite2Day) originally designed for hematologic cancer patients, targeting women with breast cancer in rural areas where symptom burden (insomnia, fatigue, distress, pain) is disproportionately high. The pilot used a single-arm design (N=15) to assess feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary changes in patient-reported outcomes.
FINDINGS: The accrual target was met within 6 months, with no attrition (15/15 completed intervention and post-treatment assessments). Acceptability was high (mean score 30.53/32). Pre-post changes in insomnia symptoms, fatigue, distress, pain, pre-sleep arousal, mindfulness, and symptom management self-efficacy all trended in the expected direction (e.g., reduced insomnia severity, improved mindfulness). Qualitative feedback led to protocol refinements (e.g., clearer mindfulness definitions, adjusted session timing).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and acceptability of Nite2Day in this population, with no major methodological flaws in this small pilot. However, the single-arm design precludes causal inference, and the lack of a control group means observed improvements could reflect placebo, natural recovery, or regression to the mean. The sample size (N=15) is too small to assess clinical significance or durability of effects. Funding sources and blinding status are not reported, and generalizability is limited by the rural, breast cancer-specific context.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary results suggest Nite2Day may be a feasible and acceptable intervention for rural breast cancer patients with insomnia and symptom clusters, warranting a randomized controlled trial to confirm efficacy. Clinicians should await stronger evidence before adopting this intervention routinely.

item.title: [6] The nucleus accumbens: an emerging modulator in anxiety disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores the role of the nucleus accumbens (NAc) in anxiety disorders, synthesizing recent evidence on neurotransmitter systems (opioid, oxytocin, endocannabinoid), glial mechanisms, and neural circuits connecting the NAc to other brain regions. It aims to highlight the NAc as a potential therapeutic target for anxiety.
FINDINGS: The review summarizes preclinical and clinical studies suggesting that the NAc modulates anxiety through interactions with the ventral tegmental area, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and medial prefrontal cortex. Pharmacological agents like ketamine and non-pharmacological interventions such as exercise and deep brain stimulation are proposed as emerging treatments targeting the NAc. However, the review does not provide quantitative effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes diverse and emerging evidence but lacks the methodological rigor of systematic reviews or meta-analyses. The conclusions are hypothesis-generating rather than definitive, and the clinical applicability of targeting the NAc remains speculative. The review highlights promising avenues for future research but does not establish causality or clinical efficacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review suggests that the NAc may be a relevant target for novel anxiety treatments, but current evidence is insufficient to guide clinical practice. Clinicians should await controlled trials before considering interventions targeting the NAc.

item.title: [32] Valerian, chamomile, and lavender for insomnia and sleep disturbance: a narrative review of mechanisms, clinical efficacy, and safety.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, clinical, and safety evidence for valerian, chamomile, and lavender in adults with insomnia disorder or sleep disturbance, prioritizing randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and guidelines from a structured literature search.
FINDINGS: Valerian showed minimal and inconsistent effects on subjective sleep quality with no consistent impact on objective sleep latency or total sleep time; evidence quality was low. Chamomile reduced Sleep Quality scores in small, heterogeneous trials, while oral lavender oil (Silexan) appeared to improve disturbed sleep primarily by reducing anxiety in patients with anxiety disorders. Evidence varied by preparation, dose, route, and population.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to small samples, heterogeneity, and methodological limitations; no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed. Findings suggest no robust support for these botanicals as alternatives to first-line insomnia treatments. High-quality, adequately powered trials with objective outcomes and adverse-event monitoring are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify recommending valerian, chamomile, or lavender as alternatives to guideline-based insomnia treatments; clinicians should discuss use with patients, acknowledging product variability and limited efficacy data.

item.title: [25] Rethinking opioid therapy in chronic pain: Role of neurobiology.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review (2015–2025) examines the neurobiological rationale for limiting long-term opioid therapy in chronic non-cancer pain and proposes a structured, multimodal, patient-centred alternative for primary care. It synthesizes systematic reviews, RCTs, and guidelines to argue that chronic pain is primarily a CNS-mediated threat response rather than persistent nociceptive input.
FINDINGS: The review cites level I evidence that long-term opioids provide at best modest benefit for chronic pain and level I evidence of harms (tolerance, dependence, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, OUD). Level II evidence frames pain as a CNS output modulated by threat appraisal. A multimodal framework (the “5 Ps”: pain education, physical activity, psychological strategies, pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic supports) is supported by level I–II evidence for improving function.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative synthesis, this paper is not designed to yield precise effect sizes or confidence intervals. Its strength lies in integrating diverse high-quality sources to challenge opioid-first paradigms. However, narrative reviews are susceptible to selection and confirmation bias. The clinical recommendations rest on mechanistic plausibility and aggregated evidence rather than head-to-head trials of the proposed framework versus usual care. External validity hinges on primary care settings where multimodal resources are available.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For patients with chronic pain, clinicians should prioritize non-opioid, function-focused strategies and reserve time-limited opioid trials for carefully selected cases with clear functional goals and close monitoring. Watch for escalating doses or paradoxical hyperalgesia as red flags.

item.title: [20] Psychological support for women following perinatal loss: a systematic review of clinical practice guidance.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) to identify and appraise psychological recommendations for supporting women’s mental health after perinatal loss (pregnancy or early postnatal death). It assessed the quality of existing guidance and synthesized recommendations to highlight gaps in psychological care.
FINDINGS: Sixteen guidelines were included; ten rated “excellent,” four “good,” and two “average” in methodological quality. Recommendations covered psychological assessment, interventions, psychosocial support, service provision, and systemic factors, but consistency and specificity varied widely. Few guidelines provided clear guidance on follow-up or long-term psychological assessment.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by heterogeneous and sometimes vague recommendations, with only moderate methodological quality in many guidelines. The lack of standardized, evidence-based follow-up protocols risks under-detection of mental health difficulties in grieving women. While the review identifies areas for improvement, it does not provide effect sizes or direct clinical outcomes, making it difficult to assess clinical impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current guidelines offer fragmented psychological support after perinatal loss. Clinicians should be aware of these gaps and consider individualized, trauma-informed follow-up, while advocating for the development of standardized, evidence-based CPGs to improve care quality.
